shots.narration: One three-hundred-kilo grizzly
can take an elk from a whole Yellowstone wolf pack, and they usually let it.
By the end, Doug stands between a bear and a tiger that eats bears.
Its dinner.
The Wolf Pack.
In June two thousand one, researchers watched six wolves surround a mother grizzly and her two cubs on the way to a carcass.
While the bears faced the wolves in front, the others rushed in and bit at them from behind.
The bears needed about twenty minutes to cover the last hundred meters to the food.
That pack had twenty more grown wolves that were not even there.
It was one of ninety-six run-ins between wolves and grizzlies recorded in the park's first eight years with wolves back.
Wherever the two meet, most fights are over food or over young.
Here's the strange part.
A grown grizzly on its own usually wins.
When it walks up to a wolf kill, the wolves tend to back off and let it eat,
especially once they've had a first meal from it.
Picture twelve people sharing a pizza, every one of them holding a knife,
and one very large man walks over and takes the box, and none of the twelve wants to go first.
The bear wins the dinner, and it still doesn't go after the wolves.
It takes the food and leaves the pack alone.
Where the two live together, each side has occasionally killed the other,
and in Yellowstone wolves have killed grizzly cubs.
Doug thinks this is unfair,
so he carries an elk leg back to the wolves, to be fair,
and for once the bear and the wolves agree on something.
Doug did not agree to this.
Doug has died. Again.
The next animal on this list weighs about fifteen kilos,
and the internet says grizzlies are scared of it.
The Wolverine.
The internet says a wolverine can chase a grizzly off its dinner,
and on paper that makes no sense at all.
A big male wolverine weighs up to about eighteen kilograms,
and a big male grizzly can weigh more than fifteen times that.
But the wolverine has the heaviest skull, the thickest jaws and the biggest teeth of any weasel on land,
and it can crack bones and frozen meat.
It is the biggest weasel on land, and it is still only about the size of a medium dog.
Taking food from one is like stealing a sandwich from a running chainsaw.
Here's the problem.
The stories of wolverines driving bears off carcasses are mostly unverified reports.
Wildlife biologists in Alaska say wolverines usually keep well away from bears and wolves,
because a meeting with either one can kill the wolverine, and wolves are the main animal that does.
In the Yellowstone area, researchers found a radio-collared wolverine that had been killed by a black bear,
next to an elk it had tried to drag away.
So a bear can win. One did, once.
Even so, a fight with an animal that does not stop is a lot of trouble for one dinner.
Doug stands next to the wolverine, for backup,
and the bear looks at both of them and leaves.
Doug is fine.
We have a feeling the bear didn't leave because of Doug.
The next animal has never chased a bear anywhere, because it just sits there,
wearing thirty thousand reasons.
Its face.
The Porcupine.
A North American porcupine carries about thirty thousand quills,
and it cannot throw or shoot a single one of them.
It doesn't need to.
The quills are only loosely attached, so they come away the moment something touches them,
and the porcupine itself weighs about nine kilograms and would mostly rather leave.
Each quill tapers to a point covered in several dozen tiny barbs,
and when the barbs get wet, they swell and help work the quill in.
A quill that has lodged keeps moving inward, about a millimeter an hour.
A porcupine is a pincushion that bites back by holding still.
The worst part is how far that goes.
Quills have been found stuck in coyotes, cougars, bears and fishers.
In the southern Yellowstone area, researchers who tracked fifty-nine cougar deaths over fifteen years
found two young cats that had hunted porcupines and died from the quills afterwards.
The best-known porcupine hunter is the fisher,
and even it has to go for the face or flip the porcupine over.
Other predators simply learn to leave them alone.
Some learn once.
Doug is wearing a porcupine costume, so the bear will leave him alone,
and it works, because the bear leaves him alone.
The quills on Doug's costume point inward.
Doug has died. Again.
The next animal doesn't need quills,
because it weighs as much as nine Dougs and it fights with its feet.
Its bones.
The Bull Moose.
In the nineteen eighties, an Alaska biologist watched a cow moose box a male grizzly
so hard that the bear went somersaulting backwards.
The bear had come for her calf.
That was a cow.
A large bull weighs up to about seven hundred kilograms.
In the fall rut, it shoves other bulls with a rack it grew in a single summer.
Moose mostly kick with their front legs,
and the hoof can come straight up, swing forward, kick out to the side, or come down on top of whatever is there.
A bull moose kick is a vending machine falling on you from shoulder height.
But that's not the whole picture.
Grizzlies do kill moose.
In one Alaska study, each adult male grizzly killed three or four adult moose a year,
and each bear killed at least five calves.
The highest kill rates came from males killing cows at calving time.
In Sweden, researchers checked thirty-two adult moose killed by brown bears.
Among the older moose, almost nine in ten were female,
and not one of the male moose the researchers had radio-collared was killed by a bear.
The bear eats moose. It mostly leaves the bulls alone.
Doug has read the numbers, so he brings the bull a moose-calf costume,
so it can see how the calves feel.
We have met this moose before. It has not changed.
That's three hundred and eighteen.
The next animal is heavier still, and in Yellowstone the bears mostly wait for it to die on its own.
The Bull Bison.
Yellowstone's grizzlies eat a lot of bison,
and almost all of that meat comes from bison that were already dead when the bear arrived.
A bull weighs up to about nine hundred kilograms, more than eleven Dougs.
Wolves and grizzlies are the only large predators of adult bison in the park,
and bison usually turn and face an attacker together, as a group.
A bull can run about fifty kilometers an hour, spin around fast, and jump about one and a half meters.
A healthy bull bison is a small car that has decided you are the road.
So the bears wait.
Bison die of hunger and disease in winter and spring, and from injuries in the rut.
In spring, when grizzlies come out of their dens,
elk, bison and other hoofed animals make up much of what they eat, and a lot of it was killed by the winter.
The uncomfortable part is how patient the bear is.
Grizzlies can take a bison calf,
but one bear researcher's verdict is that a grown bison is too big,
too well armed and too far from cover for a bear to kill outright.
So Doug waits beside a bull for it to weaken a bit, so the bear can help,
and the bison outlasts Doug.
Bison still have right of way.
So far, the bear has only risked a meal, a face full of quills or a broken bone.
The next animal is what a mother grizzly fears most.
Its cubs.
The Big Male.
In one Swedish population of brown bears, the same species as the grizzly, about a third of cubs die every year.
At least nine in ten of those deaths are caused by adult males that are not their father.
A big male grizzly can weigh more than three hundred kilograms,
which is about a tall upright piano that wants your kids gone.
Biologists call it sexually selected infanticide,
which means a male kills young that aren't his, to get a chance to mate with their mother.
The mating season runs from early May to mid-July, and that's when most of the cubs die.
But here's the clever part.
In the Swedish study, the mothers that kept their cubs stayed closer to people.
Their typical distance from houses was about seven hundred and eighty meters,
against about twelve hundred for the mothers that lost them.
Adult males there generally avoid people, so a house nearby works on them like a locked door.
In British Columbia, bear viewing pushed big males away from a river,
and the mothers with cubs spent more of their time fishing.
The animal a mother grizzly has most to fear is another grizzly, so she hides behind us.
Doug offers to babysit,
and the mother uses Doug the way she uses people, as a shield.
It works on the male.
It works less well on Doug.
Every danger so far has cost the bear its dinner, its face, its bones or its cubs,
but the next one eats bears.
Its life.
The Amur Tiger.
In the Russian Far East, tigers kill and eat brown bears, the same species as the grizzly.
A male Amur tiger weighs about one hundred and eighty to three hundred kilograms.
At the top end, that is a big touring motorbike, and it is still a cat.
Over more than twenty years, from nineteen ninety-two to two thousand thirteen, in and around the Sikhote-Alin reserve,
researchers found seven hundred and sixty-three animals killed by tigers.
About two in every hundred were bears, brown or black.
Most of the time, these tigers eat deer and wild pigs, so a bear is not on the menu every week.
Even so, bear remains turned up in roughly one in every twelve tiger droppings the researchers checked,
which is a lot of bear for a cat.
But it doesn't only go one way.
Bears there regularly feed at tiger kills, about one kill in every six in one study,
and at least eight times a bear pushed the tiger off its own kill.
The bear sometimes wins. It just doesn't always get to choose the day.
Doug stands between them in the snow, one arm out toward each,
to make sure that it stays a fair fight.
It was a fair fight, and Doug lost it.
The tiger is the one animal here that hunts the bear,
but the animal grizzlies go out of their way to avoid walks on two legs.
The Human.
Researchers in Yellowstone collected more than seventeen thousand reports of how bears reacted to people,
and in most of them, the bears stayed calm or ran away.
Grizzlies usually avoid trouble with people,
and in that study, attacks were uncommon everywhere in the park.
Before eighteen hundred, about fifty thousand grizzlies lived in what is now the lower forty-eight states.
People shot, poisoned and trapped them wherever they were found, sometimes for government bounties.
By nineteen seventy-five, only seven or eight hundred were left,
and that year they were listed as threatened.
Today there are a little over two thousand, on about six percent of their old range.
About a thousand of them live in and around Yellowstone, and most of the rest live in the northern Rockies of Montana.
If the old grizzlies were twenty-two cars in a parking lot,
today there would be one car left, and it would be parked at the far end.
Here's the honest part.
The animal grizzlies avoid most is the one that took nearly all of their land,
and it is the only one on this list that ever came close to finishing them off.
Attacks on people are rare,
and for most of history the danger has run the other way.
The last bear came for him on purpose.
This one won't.
For the first time, Doug is the scariest animal in the forest,
and he is offended,
so he follows it to make friends.
Doug has died. Again.
The cap has been avoided.
It is taking it personally.
